newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Buthelezi has his day in power.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Buthelezi has his day in power.

text.p: South African opposition leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi briefly served as acting president at the weekend and he called the appointment a sign of reconciliation between his party and the ruling African National Congress.

At the swearing-in ceremony on Saturday Buthelezi said Mandela's decision to appoint him was a gesture of peace between Inkatha and President Nelson Mandela's ANC, whose supporters have waged a bloody feud since the mid-1980s.
"I really thank the president for the trust and confidence he has shown in me," Buthelezi said.

Buthelezi, leader of the Inkatha Freedom Party and bitter rival of Mandela, handed the reins of power back on Monday morning when Deputy Minister Thabo Mbeki returned from Davos, Switzerland, where he had attended the World Economic Forum.
Mandela had also gone to Davos, leaving South Africa without its two top leaders.

"It was just a short reign, but a significant one," said Mandela's spokeswoman Priscilla Naidoo. She did not know if Buthelezi had carried out any executive tasks on Sunday, adding: "It was not a working day anyway."
The appointment of Buthelezi, a hereditary chief of the Zulu tribe who wears animal skins and carries a spear on ceremonial occasions, was greeted by some non-Inkatha supporters as a joke.
When Mandela announced his decision during a speech to the Senate on Friday, many senators broke into chuckles, the laughter slowing dying as the president resumed his seat with a straight face.

Political analyst Gerhard Mare said that despite the peace gesture to Buthelezi, fundamental issues remained to be resolved between the ANC, which holds national power, and Inkatha, which has a majority in KwaZulu-Natal province.
"I think the real issues remain conflictual. They are really to do with the powers of provinces and the role of traditional leadership -- those have not been resolved," he said.

Inkatha has refused to endorse South Africa's final post-apartheid constitution -- which comes into effect at midnight on Monday -- objecting that it does not give sufficient powers to provinces or traditional leaders like Zulu chiefs.
On the importance of Buthelezi's weekend as acting president, Mare said:

"You can look at it two ways: They've given it to him, but they've only given it to him for a day, and that was a Sunday... he took the positive way, which is part of the symbolic interplay around peace and resolving differences."
